lead: A ductile metal in a wing fitting sees two or three normal stresses plus shear. It yields when the shear, or the distortion energy, reaches the value measured in a plain tension test. Two criteria bracket the answer: maximum shear stress (Tresca), the conservative one, and distortion energy (von Mises), the usual design choice. Octahedral shear is von Mises in another dress. Stress engineers in design offices use these to turn a multiaxial state into one equivalent stress that is compared with the yield strength σ<sub>Y</sub>.
prereq: You need failure theories: maximum principal stress and strain for principal stresses and strains.

blocks.text: Tresca says yield starts when the largest shear anywhere reaches σ<sub>Y</sub>/2. In principal stresses σ<sub>1</sub> ≥ σ<sub>2</sub> ≥ σ<sub>3</sub>:
σ<sub>eq,T</sub> = max(|σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub>|, |σ<sub>2</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub>|, |σ<sub>3</sub> − σ<sub>1</sub>|) ≤ σ<sub>Y</sub>
blocks.where: σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>2</sub>, σ<sub>3</sub> are principal stresses in MPa; σ<sub>Y</sub> is the tensile yield strength in MPa.

blocks.text: In plane stress one principal stress is zero. If the other two have opposite signs, σ<sub>eq,T</sub> is their difference. If they have the same sign, it is the larger magnitude alone. Taking the difference in both cases is the commonest error.

von Mises says yield starts when distortion energy — the strain energy that changes shape, not volume — reaches its tension-test value. Hydrostatic pressure changes volume only and cannot yield a ductile metal. In principal stresses:

blocks.where: σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>2</sub>, σ<sub>3</sub> are principal stresses in MPa; the result is in MPa.

blocks.text: For plane stress with σ<sub>3</sub> = 0 this becomes σ<sub>eq,M</sub> = √(σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>²). In stress components:

blocks.where: σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> are normal stresses and τ<sub>xy</sub> is shear stress, all in MPa.

blocks.text: The 3 on τ<sub>xy</sub>² is not optional.
The octahedral plane has a normal making equal angles with the three principal axes. Its shear stress is

blocks.where: τ<sub>oct</sub> is the octahedral shear stress in MPa; σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>2</sub>, σ<sub>3</sub> are principal stresses in MPa.

blocks.text: Compare the square roots: σ<sub>eq,M</sub> = (3/√2)τ<sub>oct</sub>. So yielding when τ<sub>oct</sub> = √2 σ<sub>Y</sub>/3 is exactly von Mises, not a third independent theory. The octahedral shear carries the whole distortion; the mean stress (σ<sub>1</sub>+σ<sub>2</sub>+σ<sub>3</sub>)/3 is the normal stress on the octahedral plane; it changes volume only and leaves τ<sub>oct</sub> unchanged.

Tresca gives the larger equivalent stress, so it is conservative. The von Mises value is √(3/2) times the root-mean-square of the three principal differences, so it still cannot exceed the largest difference. Use Tresca for a quick hand check, von Mises for design and finite element work.

figure.caption: Yield loci for σ<sub>Y</sub> = 250 MPa in plane stress. The Tresca hexagon lies inside the von Mises ellipse, touching it at the six corners (uniaxial and equal biaxial stress). They differ most in pure shear (σ₂ = −σ₁): Tresca yields at 125 MPa, von Mises at 144 MPa. The worked example gives factors of 1.64 by Tresca and 1.85 by von Mises.

spec.aria: Principal stress plane with a hexagon for Tresca and an ellipse for von Mises, both passing through 250 megapascals on each axis and through 250, 250 and minus 250, minus 250. Along the pure-shear diagonal the hexagon is crossed at 125 and the ellipse at 144. The example point 106.2, minus 46.2 is inside both. A note gives the equivalent stresses 152.3 by Tresca and 135.3 by von Mises.

examples.question: A ductile panel has σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = −40 MPa, τ<sub>xy</sub> = 30 MPa and yield strength σ<sub>Y</sub> = 250 MPa. Compare Tresca, von Mises, octahedral shear and maximum principal stress; give each factor of safety.
steps: Maximum principal stress: n = 250/106.16 = 2.36, unsafe for a ductile metal.
examples.answer: Tresca gives σ<sub>eq</sub> = 152.3 MPa (n = 1.64); von Mises and octahedral shear give 135.3 MPa (n = 1.85); maximum principal stress gives n = 2.36, which is unsafe for a ductile metal.
examples.check:
import math
sx, sy, txy, sy<sub>y</sub> = 100.0, -40.0, 30.0, 250.0
avg = (sx + sy) / 2
R = math.hypot((sx - sy) / 2, txy)
s1 = avg + R
s2 = avg - R
s3 = 0.0
print(round(avg, 3))
print(round(R, 3))
print(round(s1, 3))
print(round(s2, 3))
tresca = max(abs(s1 - s2), abs(s2 - s3), abs(s3 - s1))
print(round(tresca, 3))
print(round(sy<sub>y</sub> / tresca, 3))
vm = math.sqrt(sx**2 - sx*sy + sy**2 + 3*txy**2)
print(round(vm, 3))
print(round(sy<sub>y</sub> / vm, 3))
toct = math.sqrt((s1 - s2)**2 + (s2 - s3)**2 + (s3 - s1)**2) / 3
print(round(toct, 3))
print(round(3 / math.sqrt(2) * toct, 3))
print(round(sy<sub>y</sub> / s1, 3))

traps: Using σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>2</sub> for Tresca when both in-plane principal stresses have the same sign; the larger magnitude alone governs.
Mixing plane stress (σ<sub>3</sub> = 0) with plane strain, where σ<sub>3</sub> = ν(σ<sub>1</sub>+σ<sub>2</sub>).
Comparing σ<sub>eq</sub> with ultimate strength; both criteria are yield criteria.
Using maximum principal stress for a ductile metal; it reports a safer factor than the metal actually has.

quiz.q: State the Tresca equivalent stress in principal stresses.
Write the von Mises equivalent stress in terms of σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> and τ<sub>xy</sub>.
Why does hydrostatic stress not cause yield in these theories?
quiz.a: It changes volume only. Distortion energy and octahedral shear are zero under pure hydrostatic stress.

quiz.q: Show that for plane stress with σ<sub>3</sub> = 0, von Mises reduces to √(σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>²).
quiz.a: Set σ<sub>3</sub> = 0: (σ<sub>1</sub>−σ<sub>2</sub>)² + σ<sub>2</sub>² + σ<sub>1</sub>² = 2(σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>²); divide by 2 and take the root.

quiz.q: At a point σ<sub>x</sub> = 80 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 20 MPa, τ<sub>xy</sub> = 40 MPa and σ<sub>Y</sub> = 220 MPa. Find the Tresca and von Mises factors of safety.
quiz.a: σ<sub>avg</sub> = 50 MPa, R = 50 MPa, σ<sub>1</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>2</sub> = 0, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0. Tresca: 100 MPa, n = 220/100 = 2.20. von Mises: √10 000 = 100 MPa, n = 220/100 = 2.20.

quiz.q: A point has σ<sub>1</sub> = 120 MPa, σ<sub>2</sub> = 40 MPa, σ<sub>3</sub> = −20 MPa. Find τ<sub>oct</sub> and σ<sub>eq,M</sub>.
quiz.a: Differences 80, 60, 140 MPa; sum of squares 29 600 MPa². τ<sub>oct</sub> = √29 600/3 = 57.35 MPa. σ<sub>eq,M</sub> = √(29 600/2) = 121.66 MPa.

quiz.q: A part has σ<sub>Y</sub> = 300 MPa, a finite element von Mises stress of 240 MPa and a Tresca hand check of 260 MPa. Which factor should be reported and why?
quiz.a: Quote the von Mises factor, 300/240 = 1.25, as the design value: von Mises is the normal yield criterion for ductile metals and matches their tests best. Report the Tresca factor, 300/260 = 1.15, beside it as a conservative bound; where the design rules ask for a Tresca check on fittings, it is the one that must be met.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element solvers report von Mises stress by default, and certification checks often add a Tresca hand check for fittings. Search 'Hill yield criterion' and 'Tsai–Wu' for orthotropic composite plies. Search 'Drucker–Prager' to see the same octahedral invariant used for pressure-sensitive materials.
